summary: Here we go again.
body: It's well-known that the PC ports of GTA 3, Vice City, and San Andreas were a shemozzle, thanks in part to re-used code across the trio of games, but also a general lack of care that used to be the norm when it came to PC ports. The excellent SilentPatch has long been the solution, and it's now even better thanks to a significant update that not only fixes leftover bugs, but also restores cut content that was inaccessible thanks to typos in the code. One big change you'll notice with this version of the patch is that 100 voice lines have been restored to GTA San Andreas. Some of these were only bugged in a specific circumstance—like the lines CJ says when shooting at people, which only worked if you played with a controller. Those lines will now trigger when you pull the trigger when aiming with mouse and keyboard. A lot of other dialogue that would otherwise never be heard has been restored too. body: Weird Weekend Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. body: Smartly Dressed Games, developer of the wildly popular free-to-play zombie survival sim Unturned, has released the game's source code for non-commercial use. "Unturned's source code and project files are now freely available!" the developers wrote in a Steam post . "Whether you have a new feature or total conversion in mind, the sky's the limit." The source code is available via GitHub . In an accompanying FAQ , Smartly Dressed Games explained that the reason behind the release is to further support the community's creative efforts. There are some conditions for players and modders who want to use the source code. title: GTA 6's Netflix deal forces us to ask: can you pirate an advertisement?
summary: Just when you thought videogame marketing couldn't get sillier, people are going to wind up stealing a trailer.
body: Let's be real, come August 27, the Grand Theft Auto 6 "extended look" is not going to be exclusive to Netflix for six hours as advertised. It's going to be exclusive to Netflix for however long it takes for someone to record it and distribute a torrent. You wouldn't download a car, but would you download an ad for a game about stealing cars? It would be, I've now had to consider, technically piracy to do so. After all, Netflix probably paid good money for the privilege of being the first to show the world GTA 6 gameplay, although we can only guess, because the financial terms of the deal haven't been disclosed. Aside from whatever funds exchanged hands, GTA publisher Take-Two's motivation for the deal is to signal that GTA 6 is a cultural event that transcends the gaming scene. And Netflix gets to be associated with that cultural event. I get Netflix's angle. I don't get Take-Two's, unless the payday was astronomical. Everyone already knows GTA is a big deal, and it's plain disrespectful to GTA fans to turn the gameplay trailer they've been waiting for into a money-making opportunity, especially given that many of them have already pre-ordered the game. title: FromSoftware sleuth unearths earliest footage of Demon's Souls to date: A prototype with a first person camera mode
summary: Demon's Field.
body: Seasoned FromSoftware investigator Lance McDonald has shared a recently uncovered early internal showcase of Demon's Souls , FromSoft's crucial pivot point between King's Field and Dark Souls, and the progenitor of its own subgenre. The demonstration consists of a PowerPoint presentation deck and early gameplay trailer. It was shown at "Gameshare 4," an internal Sony event held in May, 2007, almost two years before Demon's Souls' initial release in Japan. The real highlight is that two minute gameplay showcase, possibly the earliest look we've ever gotten of Demon's Souls in action, with key differences from the final game. First and most striking: There are a few sequences in a first-person camera mode à la King's Field, FromSoft's spiritual predecessor to Souls. It makes for a distinct minority of the footage's runtime, and seems to have been an optional mode you were meant to toggle between. It also ties into what strikes me as an equally profound, but less immediately grabbing difference: Demon's Souls' early 3D camera was locked behind the player model, which always faced away from the camera⁠—it reminds me of the Jedi Knight games, for a frame of reference. title: BioWare veteran says Baldur's Gate 3 was such a great sequel because it didn't try to be too much like Baldur's Gate 2
summary: Mark Darrah thinks Larian succeeded because it wasn't afraid to do its own thing.
body: Mark Darrah was a programmer on the original Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate 2, along with Neverwinter Nights and Jade Empire, and served as executive producer of the Dragon Age series from Origins through Inquisition before leaving in 2020—and coming back in 2023 to kick in on The Veilguard. He knows a thing or two about BioWare RPGs, in other words, and speaking to FRVR he said he also knows why Baldur's Gate 3 was such a great sequel—so great that it has overshadowed the games that came before it, made mounts of money, and is still among the most popular games on Steam three years after release. Darrah reckons that's a direct result of Larian's willingness to do its own thing with the sequel. Obsidian's Pillars of Eternity "feels like an Infinity Engine game," Darrah said (and he's 100% correct on that), and they're great, but Darrah says that's also a very limiting factor: "The reality is that the industry has moved on so much since then that I was like, oh yeah, this is a really faithful adaptation of that and it turns out that I didn’t actually want that anymore." title: Big Walk patch addresses voice volume complaints with restraint: 'We consider it an important part of the game's design that you can only hear players who are close to you'

body: Fantastic new puzzle game Big Walk drew some early complaints over the volume of its proximity voice chat, which was too quiet for some players and mic setups, and developer House House has now released a patch that it hopes will resolve the issue while respecting the spirit of the game. The studio has a fine line to walk, because Big Walk's primary source of friction is the challenge of communicating over distances . Voices don't carry very far, so players often have to communicate with radios, arm signals (or frantic arm waving), notes, and signs to coordinate exploration and solve puzzles. House House says that , with the new patch, Big Walk "now does a much better job of bringing players with quiet microphone setups up to the intended volume." The change does not, however, increase the distance that voices carry or introduce the option to adjust the voice and background audio levels separately. "This change makes quiet voices louder overall, so you will be louder up close, and louder at a medium distance," writes the studio. body: If one thing is true about AI, it's that there's a lot of money in it. So you'd think AI companies could buy pretty much whatever they want—but one farming family in Northern Kentucky showed that's not the case by turning down a $26 million bid. As reported by WKRC-TV Local 12 , Ida Huddleston was offered the sum for half of her 1,200-acre farmland this year, which an unnamed company would turn into an AI data center. Huddleston's daughter, Delsia Bare, reportedly said she would "stay and hold and feed a nation" and that "$26 million doesn't mean anything." AI data centers have become an ethical and ideological battleground, with Elon Musk's SpaceXAI only this week agreeing to take down 69 temporary methane turbines in Memphis over the next year in reaction to resident concerns over local disruption. title: If your AMD chipset drivers are mysteriously failing to install like mine, you'll need to manually update instead

body: Keeping on top of chipset driver updates is a boring, but necessary part of maintaining a modern PC. Unfortunately, both myself and fellow hardware nerd Jacob Fox have run into an issue with the AMD Install Manager, which attempts to install the latest chipset driver and fails miserably on both our machines. Very unhelpfully, the failed installer points to a general error page , which blitheringly suggests a whole host of vague, unrelated PC update conflicts might be to blame. I even reinstalled the entire AMD Adrenaline driver package in the hopes of an easy fix, to no avail. However, you'll be pleased to know that a manual chipset update package exists, as spotted by Reddit user Life_Recognition_963 . Simply download the individual installer at the bottom of the 8.07.16.1035 release notes page , run and reboot, and voila, the tyranny of trying to keep your machine up to date is kept at bay once again. title: Trent Reznor on Doom: 'In some ways I felt a parallel with what I was trying to do with music'
summary: A new range of Nine Inch Nails Quake merch is out.
body: A very Quake-themed QuakeCon kicked off today, with John Romero and current id studio co-director Marty Stratton speaking on a panel celebrating the shooter's 30th anniversary. A new 19-level Quake episode was announced and released during the panel, which also featured a brief livestreamed appearance from Nine Inch Nails' Trent Reznor. Reznor famously composed the music for Quake, which was a very big deal at the time. If ever there was a more 1996 cultural artefact than Quake I don't know what it could be (maybe Space Jam?). Reznor's industrial tumult definitely fit the grimier, darker, browner mood of Quake, compared to the MIDI thrash metal of Doom. I remember sometimes having to mute the music because it made me feel too tense. "When I first encountered Wolfenstein it felt impossible," Reznor said. "Nothing was like that. It was a radical departure from what I'd known as videogames. I went out and bought a PC just to play it." But it was Doom that sealed the deal. "Jump ahead a few years, Doom comes out, and it was like a bomb went off," he went on. "It was not only technologically advanced, but there wasn't anything like that. It felt like no adults were involved, nobody sai…

title: 30 years after it 'ruined id Software,' Quake gets another big update while the studio once again grapples with adversity
summary: New levels from MachineGames and archival development material have been added to the id Software classic in a free update.
body: Just a smidge over 30 years after its original release date, Quake just got a big update. MachineGames has added a new chapter to id Software's landmark 1996 successor to the Doom games, dubbed Dawn of the Machine. The 19 new levels, which join two previous MachineGames expansions, see Quake's protagonist trapped in "a dimension of endless illusion." I'm most curious about some promised new weapon variants: "the Super Axe—unleashing lightning on successive strikes—and the Laser Cannon, firing ricocheting projectiles that tear through enemies from every angle." The update also adds a gallery of archival material from Quake's development, including a handful of playable levels that were created early in development and never finished. The creative process on display is decidedly relatable, with level names like "Tim" "Tim10A," and "Tim14," and notes like, "Lots of tight hallways make navigation tough, and similarly there are many dead ends that were not completed, so it is not entirely clear what the idea was." title: John Romero says id Software once sold empty Doom boxes to Taiwanese pirates so fans there could have legit copies: 'For us, it was distribution'
summary: The id Software co-founder told the story during an opening panel at QuakeCon.
body: Doom, one of the most influential videogames of all time, was famously distributed via the shareware model: The game's first chapter was completely free, and if you liked it, you sent id Software some money and they mailed you the remaining two episodes. What would sometimes happen in those pre-online days, though, is that less-than-scrupulous resellers would offer the shareware version for sale, even though it was meant to be free. For $5 (or whatever, it's been a while), you could take home the hot new shooter from the guys who made Wolfenstein —and sure, you weren't getting the whole thing, but whatever. It's still Doom. Do you want to play it or not? You might think that id Software would take issue with people making money on their work while they received nothing, but speaking at QuakeCon today, studio co-founder John Romero said the opposite was true: They were happy to see it happen. "Please do it. Don't give us any money. Just get it out there," Romero said about people who made and sold the shareware version of Doom on floppies. "You would go to the store and you would see 10 different boxes that all had the same shareware Doom in it. I don't care. Give it to everybody, …

title: Valve explains clever shortcut for the Steam Controller's Grip Sense, and I'm starting to think it's a killer feature
summary: This seems like a solid feature for the gyro heads.
body: The Steam Controller has a pretty niche feature called Grip Sense, which is a pair of capacitive touch sensors inside the handles that can sense when you are touching them. Though you may not use it, Valve thinks you should, "because it's, like, cool," and even recommends a couple of sweet shortcuts to use with it. Valve notes that you could turn gyro controls off and on, depending on how your fingers sit on the controller, and it points out that the activation threshold is adjustable. That means you could activate a shortcut with only a slight lift of the fingers, or by taking the whole hand off the controller. Activating and deactivating gyro controls to recenter your hand is apparently called "ratcheting". Valve likens it to picking up your mouse when it hits the end of your mousepad. Effectively, if your body or hands are at an uncomfortable angle, you can take your hand off the controller to turn off gyro controls, recenter your body and turn them back on again. It's a neat function, and one I wish I had while playing Splatoon Raiders on the Nintendo Switch 2 recently (that has a recenter, but it's less natural with a dedicated button). title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword's incredible sword-fighting secret sauce explained: 'We really wanted to focus on creating this very realistic, grounded sword action'
summary: So this is how you show elite-level sword techniques.
body: During my world-exclusive hands-on preview of Onimusha: Way of the Sword in Capcom's headquarters in Osaka, Japan, I interviewed the animation director, Hiroshi Yugen, about creating the incredible sword-fighting animations for the game. When the star of the game is the legendary sword master, Miyamoto Musashi, a warrior who won over 60 duels during his lifetime, you're going to want to get these animations right. "When we get to making action in our games, the first step is always kind of self-study and learning about how to do these things and how to use these things," explains Yugen. "And then we proceed to the stages of design and motion capture. [So I] sat down and spoke with the director, and we [decided we] really wanted to focus on creating this very realistic, grounded sword action for the game, and so from the very beginning, the main goal was first to research the depths of swordplay and how to do that. "We figured it was best to speak to experts in the field, and so we were introduced to motion capture artists and action stunt coordinators at a studio called Katsugekiza Motion Capture Studio.
